title: Growth or Spending? Calgary's proposed 15% property tax increase
subtitle: A ward-level look at growth, spending, property assessments and amenities, 2021 to 2030. Independent analysis of a proposed budget; not an official City of Calgary report.
summary: The City proposes to raise the property tax it levies on existing properties by **15% in 2027**, then 10%, 7.7% and 6% (as reported). Compounded, that is **about 44% more by 2030**. A typical home would pay about **$37 a month more** in City tax in 2027 (+16%).

Population growth plus inflation adds up to **about 16%** from 2026 to 2030, so the proposed tax path is almost **three times that benchmark**. From 2027 on, the tax steps (+25.6%) move roughly in line with operating spending (+26.8%).

**Where the 2027 new money would go (proposed):** the City's 2027 operating requests ask for **$354.7 million** of new money, mostly in its **Safe city (31%) and infrastructure (29%)** themes. The largest is infrastructure maintenance: $62.4 million a year from 2027, with further yearly additions requested to 2030. About 78% is ongoing, which, if approved, would carry into later budgets. The business cases do not show how much would be paid by property tax.

**The capital plan (proposed):** about **$21 billion over 2027–2030**, with about $4.4 billion in 2027. That is **close to the $4.2 billion the City forecasts spending in 2026**, and about 1.8 times its 2025 forecast; the four-year average, about $5.25 billion a year, would be higher still. Of the $13 billion in new requests, 42% is water, wastewater and stormwater, and the ten largest requests are more than half. Large projects are built by contractors, and the City lists a tight labour market as a risk; capital that is not spent is re-timed to later years.

**Water Services is the biggest single increase** in operating spending: 43% of the increase from 2027 to 2030. It is paid mainly through water bills, not property tax. Without water, operating spending rises about 19%.

The 15% is not the same for every home. Because all homes share one tax rate, the tax follows value: estimated 2027 changes are about **+18% for semi-detached homes, +16% for detached and +8% for condo apartments** (±3 points, until 2027 assessments arrive in January). The same shift showed up on 2026 bills.

On our ward model, **five wards (5, 12, 13, 3 and 2) took about half of Calgary's growth** since 2021. They have about a third fewer transit stops and nearly three quarters fewer City recreation sites per resident than the other nine wards (counts of sites, not service quality).

**Growth or spending? Growth explains part of the increase, but the proposed tax rise is much higher than the growth-and-inflation benchmark.** That does not by itself mean the difference is waste: City costs can rise faster than consumer prices. If spent in full, the capital plan would hold spending near the level the City forecasts for 2026 (about $4.2 billion) in 2027 and above it on average to 2030, well above 2023–2025. Calgarians deserve to understand what they are paying for.
Council can still change the number: 10% instead of 15% would mean an estimated **$128 million less revenue** in 2027 (5%: about $256 million less). These are revenue gaps, not a list of cuts.

sections.heading: What is proposed
sections.text:
On November 10, 2026, City administration presented the proposed 2027 to 2030 budget. Nothing in it is approved: public submissions begin on November 23, and Council is expected to decide in December.

The proposal raises the municipal property tax levied on existing properties by 15% in 2027. News reports of the presentation give the later steps as 10% in 2028, 7.7% in 2029 and 6% in 2030; compounded, that is about 44% by 2030. Each 1% is reported as about $25.6 million, so the 2027 step is about $384 million.

The 15% is a revenue figure, not a bill figure. On the City's typical home (assessed at $706,000 in 2026 and $688,000 in 2027), the City tax goes from $229 to $266 a month, about 16%.

sections.heading: Growth and inflation against the tax path
sections.text:
Calgary has grown fast: about 1.6 million people, roughly 21% more than in April 2021 on the City's estimates. The City now forecasts growth of about 1.6% a year.

Population growth and consumer inflation together come to about 16% from 2026 to 2030. This is a benchmark, not a measure of what spending is justified: City costs such as wages, construction and ageing infrastructure can rise faster than consumer prices.

sections.heading: The proposal, broken down: new operating money (proposed)
sections.text:
The proposed 15% would raise about $384 million more in 2027. Separately, the City's 124 operating budget requests (98 with a 2027 amount) ask for **$354.7 million of new money** that year: $276.1 million ongoing (78%) and $78.6 million one-time, with 855 new full-time equivalent (FTE) positions.

The two figures should not be subtracted. The requests do not say which would be paid by property tax and which by reserves, fees or other sources, and the 15% must also cover cost growth in existing services, which the business cases do not itemize. July City documents, as reported by Global News, put the increase needed only to maintain services at 5.4% (roughly $138 million at $25.6 million per point, our arithmetic).

By the City's own themes, most of the 2027 new money falls under **Safe city (31%)** and **Reliable and sustainable infrastructure (29%)**. The single largest request is for **infrastructure maintenance: $62.4 million a year from 2027**, with further yearly additions requested to 2030. The top three (infrastructure maintenance, the Safer Together community safety plan and a low-income transit pass) are a third of the total. By the City's own rationale categories, about 49% of the money cites explicit direction from Council and 21% implicit direction.

From 2027 to 2030, yearly operating spending in the City's proposed budget data would rise by about $1.72 billion (from $6.43 billion in 2027 to $8.16 billion in 2030). Water Services is the largest piece, at $743 million (43%), paid mainly through water bills; Corporate Programs adds $579 million, Calgary Transit $164 million, and Mobility and the Calgary Police Service about $67 million each. After inflation, operating spending per resident rises about 14% from 2027 to 2030 including water, and about 7% without it.

sections.heading: The proposal, broken down: the capital plan (proposed)
sections.text:
The City proposes about **$21 billion of capital spending from 2027 to 2030**; its chief financial officer called it the largest capital program the City has seen. About $13 billion of it is in 260 new capital requests (42% of that is maintenance or replacement). The rest is capital approved in earlier budgets: the City's open data lists $6.9 billion of it for 2027–2030, and the published totals do not fully reconcile. About **$4.4 billion** would fall in 2027 (as reported). The new requests climb each year: $1.55 billion in 2027, $3.0 billion in 2028, $4.0 billion in 2029 and $4.4 billion in 2030.

**The Water Utilities service area (water, wastewater and stormwater) is the largest piece: $5.48 billion (42%)** of the new requests, led by the wastewater treatment plants program ($2.29 billion). Utilities Delivery, which also runs waste and recycling, is $5.87 billion. Roads and pathways take $1.99 billion (15%), transit $1.31 billion (10%), and corporate needs across all services (fleet, facilities, project development, land and technology) $2.10 billion (16%). Weighted by the City's own purpose split, about 42% is maintenance or replacement, 35% growth, 20% service enhancement and 3% transformative.

Most of the money sits in a few large programs. The median request is $12.1 million, and 119 of the 260 are under $10 million, but the ten largest are **54% of the total**, and the four above $500 million are all water or wastewater. In 2027, the ten largest amounts are 61% of the year's new capital.

How it would be paid: requests whose funding includes self-supported debt (repaid from utility rates or, for fleet, from charges to other City units) are 49% of the new capital; requests that include tax-supported debt, repaid from property tax, are 31%; the other 20% uses only reserves, grants or developer contributions. Requests often combine sources, so these are groupings, not exact splits. As reported, City debt would rise from $4.2 billion in 2027 to $10 billion in 2030, about 80% of its debt capacity.

The plan funds about **two-thirds (68%)** of what the same requests list as 2027–2030 infrastructure needs ($13.0 billion of $19.3 billion). This is an aggregate: 52 requests are budgeted above their own listed 2027–2030 needs, partly because of timing.

sections.heading: What pace would the plan require?
sections.text:
The City spent $1.46 billion on capital in 2023 (52.5% of budget) and $1.93 billion in 2024 (92.4%). For 2025 it forecast about $2.46 billion (91% of a $2.7 billion budget; its forecasts during 2025 moved between 91% and 101%), and the year-end figure is in a report this study could not retrieve. **The City forecasts higher spending in 2026:** the capital budget, approved at $3.7 billion, stood at $4.47 billion at June 30, 2026; the City had spent $1.38 billion (31%) and forecast about **$4.18 billion (94%)** by year-end.

If spent in full, the proposed 2027 capital budget of about $4.4 billion would be **close to the 2026 forecast (about 1.05 times)** and about 1.8 times the 2025 forecast. The four-year average of about $5.25 billion a year would be about 1.26 times the 2026 forecast and about 2.1 times the 2025 forecast. Both are the City's own forecasts: the 2025 figure was made before that year ended, and the 2026 figure can still change.

**Readiness.** By the City's own stage labels, 58% of the new capital (70% of the 2027 amount) is at Stage 4, Execute. About 22% is at Identify or Assess & Select, including the first wave of GamePLAN recreation projects, transit bus purchases and light rail vehicle replacement. A stage label is not a signed contract, and contract status is not in the budget documents. Among works in the four-year plan, the Fish Creek wastewater plant upgrade contract was awarded in January 2025 ($547 million; the contractor lists completion in 2030). The Green Line, funded mainly from earlier approvals (the new requests carry $16.6 million for it), reports more than $200 million of construction contracts awarded, station contracts expected late in 2026 and its track contract out for proposals since July 2026.

**People.** The operating requests (not the capital requests) add 855 full-time equivalent positions in 2027 and 1,926 over four years (about 1,800 as reported), mostly in transit, community safety and fire. For scale, the City's website lists 16,846 employees (basis and scope not stated). City staff, excluding police, civic partners and on-call, student and seasonal staff, rose from 13,483 at the end of 2022 to 15,751 in September 2024; the website figure and this series are on different bases. Separately, the City attributes part of its first-half 2026 operating savings to vacancies and delayed hiring (Q2 2026 quarterly report).

**Building it.** Large projects are built by contractors, for example Graham on the Fish Creek plant and PCL and Graham on Green Line packages. The City's 2026 budget lists cost escalation from a tight labour market and supply chain challenges as a risk to capital delivery, and BuildForce Canada forecasts that Alberta's construction labour force will need to add 48,800 workers by 2035, including replacing about 43,700 retirements.

**If money is not spent.** Capital budget that is not spent is re-timed to later years; in February 2025 the City moved $893 million of its 2025 budget to 2027 and later, so it now falls in or after the 2027–2030 plan period. Separately, on the operating side, consolidated expenses were 99.0%, 98.3% and 97.8% of budget in 2023 to 2025 (Annual Financial Reports). The year-end operating surpluses ($236 million, $276 million and $259 million) reflect both spending below budget and revenue above it, such as investment income, and were transferred to the Fiscal Stability Reserve the following year.

This study does not predict whether the plan will be delivered. It shows the pace the plan would require.

sections.heading: Who would pay more than 15%
sections.text:
Calgary taxes all homes at one rate, so when some homes lose value faster than others, the tax moves toward the homes that held their value. The City's own typical-home figures imply the residential rate rises about 19%; a home whose assessment falls about 3.4% would see +15%.

This already happened on 2026 bills: matching every home on the 2025 and 2026 assessment rolls, condo apartments fell about 5.9% while detached houses rose 0.8%. For 2027 we used CREB's July 2026 prices as a guide. These are estimates until the 2027 assessments are mailed in January.

sections.heading: Where Calgary grew, and amenities there
sections.text:
On the calgaryinsight.ca growth model, five wards (5, 12, 13, 3 and 2) took about half of Calgary's population growth since 2021, and about half or more under every way we tested of spreading growth that new homes do not explain. These are model estimates, not official ward counts.

Those five wards have about 33% fewer transit stops and 73% fewer City recreation sites per resident than the other nine wards. These are counts of sites, not measures of size, capacity or service quality. 311 requests are lower in these wards, which should not be read as evidence of better service.

conclusion: Growth or spending? Growth explains part of the increase: population growth and inflation come to about 16% to 2030, against about 44% for the proposed tax path. The study does not show that the difference is unnecessary; the City's costs can rise faster than consumer prices, and much of the new operating spending is water, which is paid mainly through water bills. What the numbers do show is that the proposed increase goes well beyond growth and inflation, that it would not fall evenly (houses would likely pay more than 15% and condos less), and that growth has concentrated in wards with fewer transit stops and recreation sites per resident. If spent in full, the capital plan would hold spending near the level the City forecasts for 2026 (about $4.2 billion) in 2027 and above it on average to 2030, well above 2023–2025. Calgarians deserve to understand what they are paying for; this study sets out the numbers behind that choice.
method: Population: calgaryinsight.ca growth model. Every home on the City's assessment roll by community and year built, times 2021 Census people per home, scaled to the City's own monthly estimate. Ward figures are estimates.
Spending: City of Calgary 2027 to 2030 budget open data (operating spending after recoveries), compared on matching periods with the City's population and inflation forecasts.

Who pays: the residential rate change implied by the City's typical-home figures, applied to every home on the 2026 roll by type, using CREB July 2026 price changes. Back-tested on 2026 bills (error up to about 2.7 points).
Amenities: City recreation sites and transit stops in each ward divided by ward residents; 311 requests per 1,000 residents.
The full technical report (PDF) lists every formula, every source with a link, and how to repeat each figure.
limitations: 2027 assessments are not published yet; the estimates by home type and ward are indicative (about ±3 points).
The 2028 to 2030 tax steps and the $25.6 million per 1% figure come from news reports of the City's presentation.
Ward populations are model estimates, not official ward counts.
Site counts do not measure capacity or service quality; with 14 wards, patterns are descriptive only.
Consumer inflation is a benchmark; the City's own costs can rise faster.
